Note that due to reader requests, I've decided to break up my weekly portfolio updates into three parts: commentary, economic update, and portfolio summary, stats, and watch lists. This is to avoid excessively long articles and maximize the utility to my readers.
This week's commentary looks at why oil prices are likely to recover from their recent bear market, and three deeply undervalued, high-yield blue-chips you should buy before they do .
There is no economic update this week because of Thanksgiving and family obligations.
Introduction First, let me be very clear that this is my personal portfolio tailored to my specific financial situation, risk profile, time horizon, and personality traits. I am not recommending anyone mirrors this portfolio. My situation is that I'm about to turn 32, but consider this portfolio an income-focused retirement one (though in a taxable account, so I can use modest amounts of margin).
I'm also working full-time (self-employed) and am thus able to continually add to this portfolio. I do not plan to actually tap the portfolio's income stream for 14-20 years when I plan to move my family (and help support my parents) to the promised land of my people (retired dividend investors): Coastal Florida.
What this portfolio can be used for is investing ideas; however, this portfolio includes high-, low-, as well as medium-risk stocks, so it's up to each individual to do their own individual research and decide which, if any, of my holdings, are right for you.
For a detailed explanation of my methodology, please read my introductory article to the EDDGE (Eternal Daily Dividend Growth Experiment) 4.0 portfolio. However, keep in mind that the portfolio is not static, and both it and the underlying investment strategy will evolve and adapt over time. This is because a changing world, new knowledge, and more experience will cause me to fine-tune it over coming years and decades to maximize my income and total returns.
Also, note that this is currently a highly sector concentrated portfolio. That's because I received my professional training working at The Motley Fool's energy desk, specializing in midstream MLPs (and also lots of renewable energy yieldCos). Thus my comfort with these high-yield and very fast-growing industries. Since moving to Seeking Alpha (and becoming an analyst for Simply Safe Dividends), I've branched out into covering all industries. I now look at about 200 companies per year in detail. I spent most of the first year building out full positions in deeply undervalued midstream stocks, and am now diversifying into other sectors (during each market downturn).
The bottom line is that researching dividend stocks is both my greatest passion and my profession. Thus, you should only use these updates as sources of ideas, but not mirror them exactly unless your risk profile/time horizon/goals very closely match my own.
Some Capital Recycling This Week Due To Incredible Buying Opportunities Right now I have several goals for this portfolio. One of those is to continue diversifying into non-energy stocks since my initial positions in MLPs/midstream stocks (the most undervalued source of generous, safe, and fast-growing income) are now complete. Another is deleveraging ahead of either the next market downturn (after this one is finished) or the next bear market (depending on whether the yield curve indicates another recession is imminent ). Finally, my core portfolio goal is to opportunistically take advantage of the best long-term investment opportunities I find, based on the combination of:
safe yield fast long-term dividend growth undervaluation Due to the need to deleverage at the moment (only buy on margin when there's blood in the street) that means making new investments, either adding to existing non-energy positions or buying new undervalued dividend growth stocks, requires selling existing positions. The goal is to lock in earlier profits from investments I made during the last correction. All while boosting expected total returns and if possible, increasing my yield at the same time.
The first buy I made this week was adding to Clearway Energy ( CWEN ), the yieldCo formally known as NRG Yield. Thanks to PG&E's ( PCG ) 60% slide this week on fears that it would be liable for the Camp Fire (and thus potentially bankrupted) all yieldCos sold off in a blind panic. The market feared that some of the power purchase agreements or PPAs it had on projects contracted to PG&E would be defaulted on.
CWEN plunged 11% last week in a single day, which is when I decided to add to it, thus boosting my portfolio yield, and lowering my cost basis significantly. Note that later that week PG&E soared over 30% in a single day when the California Utility Commission indicated it would work with the utility to prevent its bankruptcy. NextEra Energy Partners ( NEP ), another yieldCo I own, reiterated its previous payout growth guidance, indicating that even in a worst-case bankruptcy of PG&E the PPAs would likely still be honored. That's the assumption I made when increasing my position in the stock. To fund that purchase, I sold my QTS Realty ( QTS ) at an 11% profit (not counting dividends). Thus I was able to trade a lower yielding stock for a higher-yielding and more undervalued one, with slightly better long-term total return potential.
The second buy this week (and the only new stock) was Innovative Industrial Properties ( IIPR ). This is the only cannabis REIT in America and the hands-down best way to profit from the explosive growth in this new and rapidly growing industry . The reason I like IIPR so much is that the triple net leases it has with medical cannabis growers are insanely profitable and will only get more so over time (due to rapidly rising economies of scale).
cash yields on new properties: 15% (management target, 15.7% average), industry average 5% to 8% annual rent escalators 3% to 4% (industry average 1% to 2%) YTD AFFO margin: 60% and set to rise to the highest in the triple net lease industry Note that IIPR's TTM revenue is just $12 million and SG&A fees are about $5.5 million per year. The REIT is funding 100% of its growth with accretive equity (no debt because no one will buy cannabis-related bonds) and in the last four months, it purchased three new facilities. IIPR has enough cash left to acquire two new facilities (bringing it to 12) which it will likely do by the next earnings release. Last quarter revenue grew 150% and analysts expect long-term AFFO/share growth of 40% from IIPR, which if attained would make it among the fastest growing companies in America.
Personally, I think analysts are suffering from cannabis hyper-bullishness but think long-term 20% growth is attainable. The dividend should grow at 15% to 20% CAGR which will allow the REIT to lower its payout ratio (88% in 2018) so it can retain more cash flow to grow (2020 AFFO payout ratio forecast to be 74%). That's important because of the reason that IIPR is a high-risk stock.
While the business model itself is low-risk (long-term leases of 15 years and tenant pays maintenance, insurance, and property taxes), cannabis is still illegal at the Federal level. That means that IIPR exists in a unique niche right now. Because of the risk of a Fed crackdown on its customers, bond investors won't buy any of its debt (thus it has no plans to issue any). Rather the REIT must fund all growth with equity, which thankfully has a cost of equity of about 3.1% right now. But to live up to its amazing long-term return potential (possibly 10X your money over the next decade), IIPR needs the status quo to remain intact.
That means that Federal legalization of cannabis would likely be bad since it would mean that its tenants can demand much lower cap rates on their properties (plus lower annual rental escalators). What's more IIPR's current small size (just 10 properties and under $500 million market cap) means it absolutely lacks any competitive advantages in terms of access to low-cost capital. The day cannabis becomes legal larger industrial or triple net lease REITs will start replicating its business model and possibly buy it out (if it gets big enough first).
Meanwhile, if the share price were to plunge (cannabis stocks are crazy volatile) then its main funding source would be cut off. And if the Fed's did end the current policy of ignoring the 32 states (plus DC) that allow medical/recreational cannabis, then its tenants might be bankrupted.
So while the dividend remains covered by its fast-growing cash flow and the balance sheet is pristine, IIPR remains a high-risk stock. Fortunately, the valuation is actually not risky (assuming the status quo holds up). On a forward P/AFFO basis, the REIT trades at about 17X AFFO which is in line with the rest of the REIT sector. I estimate the shares are about 25% undervalued based on its realistic growth potential, and potentially up to 55% undervalued if analysts are right about how fast its cash flow (and dividend) will grow.
As a high-risk stock, I'm limited to a 2.5% stake in my portfolio. That would be about $8,0000 but since I only had two candidate stocks I could sell I had to settle for a $5,000 initial position (I bought it the day before the stock shot up 5.5%). That $5K came from selling Dominion Midstream Partners ( DM ) and Algonquin Power & Utilities Corp (NYSE: AQN ).
Dominion in an MLP that's being acquired by Dominion Energy ( D ) in early Q1 2019, and thus I was going to sell it to roll the proceeds into AQN which was recently down 10%. Thus the plan was to lower my cost basis on a fast-growing utility with 16% long-term return potential. However, AQN recently recovered 8% and since IIPR's total return potential is 20% to 25% I decided to sell both stocks to take an initial position in my third and final high-risk stock.
For risk management purposes, I limit myself to three high-risk stocks and no more than 7.5% of invested capital. My three high-risk stocks (UNIT, OHI, and IIPR) actually make up about 4.8% of my portfolio at the moment.
Thanks to these three sales and two buys I was able to slightly boost my overall portfolio stats:
yield: 6.1% 1-year dividend growth rate: 21.2% five-year average dividend growth rate: 16.0% average valuation (per dividend yield theory): 30% discount to fair value The Best Dividend Growth Stocks You Can Buy Today This group of 20 dividend growth blue chips represents what I consider the best stocks you can buy today. They are presented in four categories, sorted by most undervalued (based on dividend yield theory using a 5-year average yield).
High yield (4+% yield) Fast dividend growth Dividend Aristocrats Monthly dividend stocks Note there may be some overlap between these groups. To help with further research, I've linked to my articles for each recommendation (those not behind a paywall).
The goal is to allow readers to know what are the best low-risk dividend growth stocks to buy at any given time. You can think of these as my "highest-conviction" recommendations for conservative income investors. Note these are not meant to represent a diversified or complete portfolio, but merely highlight the best opportunities for low-risk income investors available in the market today.
The valuations are determined by dividend yield theory, which Investment Quality Trends, or IQT, has proven works well for dividend stocks since 1966, generating market-crushing long-term returns with far less volatility.
(Source: Investment Quality Trends )
That's because, for stable business income stocks, yields tend to mean-revert over time, meaning cycle around a relatively fixed value approximating fair value. If you buy a dividend stock when the yield is far above its historical average, then you'll likely outperform when its valuation returns to its normal level over time.
For the purposes of these valuation-adjusted total return potentials, I use the Gordon Dividend Growth Model or GDGM. Since 1956, this has proven relatively accurate at modeling long-term total returns via the formula: Yield + dividend growth. That's because, assuming no change in valuation, a stable business model (doesn't change much over time) and a constant payout ratio, dividend growth tracks cash flow growth.
The valuation adjustment assumes that a stock's yield will revert to its historical norm within 10 years (over that time period, stock prices are purely a function of fundamentals). Thus, these valuation total return models are based on the formula: Yield + projected 10-year dividend growth (analyst consensus, confirmed by historical growth rate) + 10-year yield reversion return boost.
For example, if a stock with a historical average yield of 2% is trading at 3%, then the yield is 50% above its historical yield. This implies the stock is (3% current yield - 2% historical yield)/3% current yield = 33% undervalued. If the stock mean-reverts over 10 years, then this means the price will rise by 50% over 10 years just to correct the undervaluation.
That represents a 4.1% annual total return just from valuation mean regression. If the stock grows its cash flow (and dividend) at 10% over this time, then the total return one would expect from this stock would be 3% yield + 10% dividend (and FCF/share) growth + 4.1% valuation boost = 17.1%.

Note that the 10-year dividend growth figures are artificially low because my tracking software doesn't average in anything that hasn't existed for those time periods. Some of my holdings have IPO-ed in the last five years, and so, the 1-year and 5-year growth rates are the most accurate. These figures are purely organic growth rates and assume no dividend reinvestment. The dividend declines during the Financial Crisis were due to three of the REITs I own cutting their dividends (57 REITs did during the Great Recession). Fortunately, since then the sector has deleveraged and now sports the lowest debt/capital ratio (30%) in its history. That means that during the next recession most REITs will NOT cut their payouts, especially the ones I own.
The long-term goal is to maintain a 10+% organic income growth rate.
Projected Portfolio Dividends Over Time (Source: Simply Safe Dividends) (Note: Assumes no dividend reinvestment, just organic growth that slows gradually over time (constant holdings))
Even assuming no dividend reinvestment (I do that manually) and that I never sell anything I own (if growth slows and I find better opportunities), this portfolio would become an income powerhouse. And even if I were to not add to the portfolio at all with fresh savings within 20 years, I would have achieved my goal of financial independence.
Over the long term, my goal is about 5% portfolio yield, with about 10% long-term dividend growth over time. In order to maintain that, I may have to recycle some holdings when they no longer meet my needs.
For perspective, the S&P 500 yields 1.9% and its 20-year median annual dividend growth rate has been 6.4% . So, the goal is about to triple the market's yield, with about 4% faster dividend growth. Since 1871, the S&P 500 has generated annual total returns of 9.2% . The market's historical inflation-adjusted total return has been 7.0%.
Even assuming no valuation multiple expansion (my deeply undervalued portfolio always remains so), this portfolio should easily be capable of about 15% un-levered total returns over time. Factoring in multiple expansion (which is already starting to happen for some of my stocks) and 25% leverage, the returns could be even greater, potentially north of 20% annualized net levered returns.

Bottom Line: Sometimes Taking Advantage Of Great Opportunities Means Making Hard Choices While buy and hold investing is the best option over time, sometimes to take advantage of great investing opportunities we need to lock in profits and redeploy the capital into stocks that boost our portfolios primary goals. In this case, I was able to maintain the same yield as before but boost my portfolio's dividend growth rate and thus total return potential.
I'm now all out of sellable stocks since my early winners aren't likely to match up with good capital recycling opportunities. For example, Simon Property Group is a grade A blue-chip that's still deeply undervalued and Uniti Group represents a 15% YOC for me. Omega Healthcare and EPR are trading at roughly fair value at the moment however my yield on cost for those is so high that it would require a truly remarkable opportunity to get me to sell them. While I'm not opposed to selling 50% of my position and retaining the other half (let your winners run) those positions aren't really large enough to allow for that.
But the stock market is full of surprises and if such an opportunity pops up that I act on, I'll make sure to tell you about it. That includes a detailed explanation of my rationale, to hopefully point out great opportunities that might help you achieve your own long-term financial goals.
